Figure(s): John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev
Problem: A confrontation over Soviet missiles in Cuba risked rapid escalation.
Response: Used a quarantine, public and private communications, and reciprocal concessions to create an exit.
When J should retrieve: High-stakes bargaining where both sides need an off-ramp and public positions differ from private flexibility.
Outcome / caveat: A celebrated case, but causal credit is distributed and some terms remained secret at the time.
Decision: Whether to answer the discovery of Soviet missile sites in Cuba with an air strike and invasion, or with a naval quarantine backed by the threat of further military action.
Context before: In July 1962 Khrushchev and Castro had secretly agreed to place Soviet missiles in Cuba, and on 14 October a U-2 photographed missile sites under construction. Kennedy was shown the photographs on the morning of 16 October and met in secret with his advisers for several days. Two principal courses were put to him: an air strike and invasion, or a naval quarantine with the threat of further military action. All the Joint Chiefs of Staff argued for an air strike, while other advisers favoured stern warnings. On 21 October General Walter Sweeney of Tactical Air Command told him an air strike could not guarantee 100% destruction of the missiles.
Goals: end the missile deployment | avoid nuclear war | keep the discovery secret until the public address | maintain credibility with allies and the public
Available information: U-2 photography of sites under construction | several days of secret adviser meetings | an air-strike assessment that complete destruction could not be guaranteed
Unknowns at the time: whether Khrushchev would accept a deal | whether the missiles were already operational | how Soviet forces in Cuba would respond | how allies and the U.S. public would react to each option
Constraints: nuclear escalation risk | alliance and domestic politics | secrecy until the televised address | time pressure while sites neared completion
Options: Air strike to destroy the missiles, followed by invasion | Stern warnings to Cuba and the Soviet Union | Naval quarantine with the threat of further military action (chosen, ordered 22 October)
Outcome: On 28 October Khrushchev publicly stated the missiles would be dismantled, in exchange for a U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba; in a separate deal kept secret for more than twenty-five years, the United States agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey, which it did in April 1963. The quarantine ended on 20 November 1962. The arms race continued, but a White House–Kremlin "Hotline" was set up and the Limited Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed on 25 July 1963.
Disputed points: Tom Blanton (National Security Archive) argues the Jupiter element that ended the crisis was kept secret for decades while the White House promoted a narrative that the Soviets had backed down, and that the crisis lasted 59 days rather than 13. The JFK Library notes that the Turkey deal stayed secret for more than twenty-five years. How credit divides between Kennedy, his advisers and the back channel is debated, but no named historian on that question was opened.
Analogy limits: nuclear superpower dyad in 1962 | superpower credibility and back channels | intelligence specific to U-2 photography
Mechanism tags: de_escalation | face_saving_exit | signalling | information_asymmetry | escalation | deterrence
Horizon: About two weeks (16–28 October 1962); 59 days counting until the warheads left (NSArchive)
Research notes: MERGED from both research passes. From the other pass: the 21 October Sweeney briefing, the 25-year secrecy, the arms-race and LTBT outcome. From mine: the State Department milestone (opened in my pass, failed in the other), the NSArchive dissent, the Joint Chiefs’ position. Khrushchev’s birth date differs between passes (Britannica: 17 April [5 April O.S.] 1894; other pass: 15 April); age 68 either way. Main figure Kennedy. The “groupthink” debate mentioned in the other pass has no opened source and was dropped from Disputed points.

Decision moment: Persuading Qin to leave the siege of Zheng
Problem: A small state faced a stronger coalition of Qin and Jin.
Response: Argued that Qin's interests diverged from Jin's and that strengthening Jin would not benefit Qin.
When J should retrieve: A weaker actor faces a coalition whose members have misaligned incentives.
Outcome / caveat: Speech details survive through later textual tradition and require careful source treatment.
Decision: Whether Zheng, besieged by Jin and Qin, should send the aged Zhu Zhiwu by night to persuade the Earl of Qin to abandon the siege.
Context before: According to the Zuo zhuan (Duke Xi, year 30), in the ninth month the rulers of Jin and Qin besieged Zheng, citing its lack of courtesy to Jin and its double-dealing with Chu; Jin camped at Hanling and Qin south of Fan. The minister Yi Zhihu told the Earl of Zheng the state was in danger and that if Zhu Zhiwu were sent to the ruler of Qin, the armies would withdraw. Zhu Zhiwu declined, saying that even in his prime he had been unequal to others and was now too old. The Earl of Zheng took the blame for not employing him earlier and warned that Zheng’s fall would harm him too, and Zhu Zhiwu agreed to go.
Goals: secure the withdrawal of the besieging armies | preserve Zheng's survival
Available information: the separate camps and commands of Jin and Qin | Jin's record toward Qin (having promised territory and then fortified it) | the advice of Zheng's own ministers
Unknowns at the time: whether the Earl of Qin would receive the envoy | what Qin would demand for withdrawing | how Jin would respond if Qin withdrew
Constraints: Zheng's military weakness | the besieging armies' proximity to the city | the envoy's age
Options: Send Zhu Zhiwu by night to persuade the Earl of Qin (chosen) | Zhu Zhiwu declines the mission on grounds of age (his first answer)
Outcome: Let down from the wall by rope at night, Zhu Zhiwu argued that destroying Zheng would enlarge Jin, Qin’s neighbour, rather than Qin. The Earl of Qin made a covenant with Zheng, left three officers (Qizi, Fengsun, Yangsun) to garrison it, and went home. Duke Wen of Jin declined to attack the departing Qin army, saying it would be unkind to strike one whose strength he had relied on, and also withdrew.
Disputed points: The account survives only in the Zuo zhuan. Britannica says it was once attributed to Zuo Qiuming but is now considered an anonymous early Warring States compilation; the Good Works Library introduction says the text was most likely drawn together from older court records and court stories in the fourth century BCE, so the speech is a literary record. D. K. Schneider reads the episode as "a triumph of rhetoric over reality". Whether Qin withdrew because of the speech or for its own reasons is not settled by these sources.
Analogy limits: Spring-and-Autumn interstate politics | single transmitted text with literary speeches | envoy persuasion in a besieged-city setting
Horizon: one night
Geography: Zheng (besieged city, modern Henan) | Qin camp south of Fan
Research notes: MERGED. The other pass reached the classical Chinese text on ctext.org (blocked in my pass); my pass has D. K. Schneider’s English translation (War on the Rocks) and Britannica on the Zuo zhuan. The two now corroborate each other on every narrative step. Rule 6: source text is the Zuo zhuan. Figure(s): Nelson Mandela and the negotiating teams
Problem: Deep mistrust and political violence threatened a negotiated transition.
Response: Continued bargaining while building arrangements for political transition and future shared institutions.
When J should retrieve: Opponents must coexist after the decision; outright victory is unrealistic.
Outcome / caveat: Do not reduce a multilateral, collective transition to one heroic actor.
Theme tags: Transition bargaining | Negotiating under violence | Institutional design
Decision: Whether to break off negotiations with the National Party government after the Boipatong massacre, and on what terms to return to them.
Context before: Negotiations had opened with the Groote Schuur Minute in May 1990, after the ANC was unbanned and Mandela released. The first CODESA plenary began in December 1991, when about 228 delegates from nineteen parties signed a Declaration of Intent, and in early 1992 over 68% of voters in a whites-only referendum backed continued negotiation. At CODESA 2 in May 1992 the parties deadlocked over the interim government and the constitution; the NP had proposed that constitutional decisions require a 70 percent majority. On 17 June 1992 more than forty residents of Boipatong were massacred, and there were reports of police collusion in the attack.
Goals: an undivided, non-racial democratic South Africa | a new constitution | an end to political violence | an interim government acceptable to all parties
Available information: the Declaration of Intent's constitutional principles | the working groups' deadlock positions | white referendum support for negotiations | the NP's minority-veto proposal and the ANC's counter-proposals
Unknowns at the time: whether violence could be contained | whether the security forces were complicit in it | whether decision thresholds could be agreed | whether excluded parties (PAC, Conservative Party, AZAPO) would ever join
Constraints: ongoing political violence | the NP's domestic base and the white referendum | exclusion of the PAC, Conservative Party and AZAPO | the unresolved design of an interim government
Options: Break off bilateral and CODESA negotiations and pursue mass action (chosen, June 1992) | Continue negotiations as before (the alternative the ANC statement rejects) | Keep the Ramaphosa–Meyer back channel open (chosen alongside) | Return to talks on the basis of a Record of Understanding (chosen, September 1992)
Outcome: The ANC issued fourteen demands and ran a mass-action campaign, including a two-day general strike that drew about 4 million workers; 28 ANC protesters were later killed by the Ciskei Defence Force at Bisho. Behind-the-scenes Meyer–Ramaphosa meetings in September 1992 and the Record of Understanding signed by Mandela and De Klerk on 26 September put negotiations back on track. The Multi-Party Negotiating Forum began on 1 April 1993 and ratified an interim constitution on 18 November 1993 (Act 200 of 1993). In the election of 27 April 1994 the ANC won 62%, and Mandela was sworn in as president on 10 May 1994.
Disputed points: Responsibility for the violence: the ANC accused the government of complicity, while the O’Malley overview records only "reports of police collusion". Why talks resumed: the UNESCO nomination calls it "a widely held belief" that the Meyer–Ramaphosa relationship played a big role; SAHO’s Chapter 8 credits "the maturity of the negotiators" and calls the Record of Understanding "a historic turning point". No named historian’s view was opened on either question.
Analogy limits: negotiated transition with an incumbent regime | timing of the Cold War's end | high levels of organized political violence
Mechanism tags: signalling | escalation | preserving_options | de_escalation | coalition_building | institutional_constraint
Horizon: About three months for the break-off and return (June–September 1992), within a negotiation lasting 1990–1994
Geography: Kempton Park and Johannesburg, South Africa
Research notes: MERGED. Decision narrowed (my pass) to the Boipatong break-off and return; the other pass framed it as persisting after the CODESA 2 deadlock — both are now in the Options. Date and Age updated to June–September 1992 and 73–74. SOURCE ERROR TO CHECK: the UNESCO nomination dates the National Peace Accord to 14 September 1990; it is widely dated 14 September 1991, so the Accord is left out of Context until checked. CODESA I start date differs: SAHO 21 December 1991; UNESCO 20 December 1991; SAHO timeline mentions talks on 29–30 November. Boipatong toll: SAHO "more than forty"; the other pass reports an O’Malley figure of 15 that was not quoted — leave as disputed.

Figure(s): Jimmy Carter, Anwar Sadat, and Menachem Begin
Problem: Egyptian and Israeli positions were difficult to reconcile under domestic and security constraints.
Response: Used intensive mediation, separate discussions, and a package framework.
When J should retrieve: Direct talks are stuck and a mediator can clarify priorities or bundle concessions.
Outcome / caveat: The accords did not resolve the wider Arab–Israeli conflict.
Decision: Whether to convene a three-way summit at Camp David and mediate it personally, rather than leave Egypt and Israel to their stalled direct talks or return to a Geneva conference.
Context before: Carter had entered office hoping to reconvene the Geneva Conference established in December 1973. Israel’s May 1977 election brought Begin’s Likud to power, and Begin appeared intractable on exchanging land for peace. In November 1977 a frustrated Sadat announced he was willing to go to Jerusalem, but the direct Egypt–Israel talks that followed in December made no substantive progress. By 30 July 1978, with Sadat expressing disappointment and a desire to cut off direct contacts, Carter decided to call a summit, which was formally announced on 8 August. The main sticking points were Israeli settlements and airbases in Sinai, Gaza and the West Bank, and how UN Security Council Resolution 242 applied to the territories.
Goals: break the negotiating deadlock | reach a detailed Egyptian–Israeli peace agreement
Available information: a U.S.-drafted treaty text serving as basis for negotiations | the parties' stated positions on withdrawal and autonomy | Sadat's expressed frustration and desire to cut direct contacts
Unknowns at the time: whether Begin would sign | whether the frameworks would satisfy other Arab states, Jordan and the Palestinians | whether a treaty could be concluded quickly after the summit
Constraints: Begin's coalition politics and settlement policy | Sadat's obligations to other Arab states | the two-week retreat format and the collapse of trilateral sessions
Options: Reconvene the Geneva Conference (Carter’s earlier aim) | Leave Egypt and Israel to continue direct talks | Three-way summit at Camp David with U.S. mediation (chosen)
Outcome: The summit ran from 5 to 17 September 1978. When the trilateral format became impossible to sustain, Carter and Vance met each delegation separately, working from a U.S. draft text revised many times, and on 15 September Carter proposed by letter to conclude within two days. The summit produced two Framework documents. After six more months of negotiation the Egyptian–Israeli Peace Treaty was signed on 26 March 1979 and has held, but later Palestinian autonomy talks produced little.
Disputed points: The National Archives exhibit credits Carter’s personal mediation for keeping talks moving; the Office of the Historian attributes the failure of the autonomy talks to Palestinian non-participation, the gap between the parties and Carter’s reduced involvement, and calls the Accords the "high-water mark" of his peace process. The Accords failed to win support from Jordan or Saudi Arabia.
Analogy limits: U.S. superpower mediation | two-state negotiation with excluded third parties | leader-specific relationships in 1978
Horizon: 13 days (5–17 September 1978)
Research notes: MERGED. Decision taken from the other pass (convening the summit), which matches the original case row; my pass’s decision (switching to separate meetings mid-summit) is kept as the mechanism in Outcome. The widely told story that Sadat threatened to leave Camp David could not be sourced in either pass. The accords’ text (AU-hosted PDF) and FRUS meeting memoranda (docs 30–56) were not read.

Decision moment: Settlement with Austria after the Austro-Prussian War
Problem: Victory created pressure to impose harsher terms on Austria.
Response: Advocated a comparatively limited peace that preserved Austria as a future diplomatic actor.
When J should retrieve: The user has leverage over a defeated rival but may need future cooperation.
Outcome / caveat: Do not treat restraint as altruism; it served Prussian strategy.
Theme tags: Leadership | Restraint after victory | Timing | Post-victory settlement | Restraint
Decision: Whether to press for a quick peace with Austria on terms that took none of its territory, or continue toward Vienna and seek harsher terms as the king and generals wanted.
Context before: Prussia defeated Austria at Königgrätz on 3 July 1866, and armistice negotiations opened at Nikolsburg three weeks later. King Wilhelm I and his generals wanted to march on Vienna, and the king also regarded the annexation of Saxony as a legitimate war trophy. France had made it known that it expected any agreement to preserve Saxony’s territorial integrity and independence. Wilhelm reluctantly agreed that the war should be concluded as quickly as possible, before Britain and Russia might intervene.
Goals: End the war before outside powers intervened | Avoid humiliating Austria | conclude peace quickly | reorganize Germany north of the River Main under Prussian leadership without Austria | avoid intervention by other great powers
Available information: The scale of the Königgrätz victory | Signs of French interference after the battle | the military situation after Königgrätz | French expectations regarding Saxony | the king's and army's appetite for annexations | Italy's claim to Venetia under the April 1866 alliance
Unknowns at the time: Whether France or other powers would intervene militarily | How Austria would act after the peace | whether Britain or Russia would intervene | whether Austria would accept the terms | whether France would press further demands
Constraints: The king’s authority and his demands | The military staff’s reluctance | The risk of a wider war | threat of British or Russian intervention | French demands on Saxony's integrity | the king's and military leadership's preference for annexations | the Italian alliance commitment on Venetia
Options: Continue the war and march on Vienna (king and generals) | Annex Saxony (pressed by Wilhelm; ruled out under French pressure) | Quick peace taking no Austrian territory (chosen, urged by Bismarck)
Outcome: Under the Preliminary Peace of Nikolsburg (26 July 1866) Austria’s territory remained intact apart from Venetia, but it paid 40 million thalers, recognised the dissolution of the German Confederation and accepted a new organisation of Germany without Austria. The Treaty of Prague formally ended hostilities on 23 August. Prussia annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau and Frankfurt, and formed the North German Confederation in 1867.
Disputed points: Motives: GHDI’s editors argue the generous terms aimed to attract the south German states into a future union; the British ambassador Lord Loftus wrote on 4 August 1866 that Prussia could not risk a war with France; Britannica gives both fear of intervention and a wish not to humiliate Austria. How lenient the terms were is itself contested: GHDI calls the indemnity "substantial", Britannica calls it "modest".
Analogy limits: The victor had an overwhelming military position | A credible third-party intervention threat | The defeated rival remained a great power with whom future dealings were expected | The key dispute was internal (minister against king and generals) | 19th-century great-power system | monarchical court politics | limited war after a quick, decisive battle
Horizon: About seven weeks (3 July – 23 August 1866)
Research notes: MERGED. The other pass reached GHDI (germanhistorydocs.org, including the treaty articles and Loftus’s letter), which was robots-blocked on the old ghi-dc.org domain in my pass; I re-checked three GHDI passages and they match. My pass contributes Britannica’s statement that the king and generals wanted to march on Vienna (which the other pass could not source) and the north German annexations. Bismarck’s memoir body text still not opened.

Figure(s): Georges Clemenceau and the Allied peacemakers
Problem: The victors had to set security, territorial, military, and reparations terms after World War I.
Response: Pursued French security within a negotiated Allied settlement that imposed major constraints on Germany.
When J should retrieve: Post-victory settlement where punishment, deterrence, reconstruction, and future stability conflict.
Outcome / caveat: Label disputed: historians contest how harsh the treaty was, how much Clemenceau shaped it, and its causal role in later conflict.
Theme tags: Leadership | Post-victory settlement | Security guarantees | Collective bargaining
Decision: Whether to drop France’s demand for an autonomous Rhineland in exchange for Allied occupation, demilitarisation and an Anglo-American guarantee.
Context before: The Paris Peace Conference convened in January 1919, and although nearly thirty nations took part, the "Big Four" of Britain, France, the United States and Italy dominated it. The United States was not bound by the Allies’ earlier secret territorial agreements, and Wilson opposed many of them, which led to frequent disagreements. For France, security against a future German attack came first, and the French brief prepared by Tardieu argued that an autonomous Rhineland would serve both self-determination and defence. The British and Americans rejected that brief in the strongest terms, while Clemenceau was under attack at home from Poincaré, Foch and parliament.
Goals: Security against a future German attack | Reparations and territorial losses that would keep Germany from rising again | French security against a recovered Germany | reparations for war damage | enforcement of the settlement
Available information: British and American opposition to detaching the Rhineland | Domestic criticism from Poincaré, Foch and parliament | the armistice outcome | Allied secret agreements on territories | Wilson's League of Nations proposals | the Allied coalition's relative power
Unknowns at the time: Whether the U.S. Senate would ratify the treaty and the guarantee | Whether Germany would comply | what reparations amount would be set (determined only in 1921) | whether the U.S. Senate would ratify | Germany's capacity to pay | how durable the settlement would prove
Constraints: Need for agreement with Britain and the United States | Domestic political attack | need for Big Four unity | Wilson's opposition to pre-existing arrangements | domestic French expectations after the war | absence of Russia and the defeated powers from the table
Options: Autonomous Rhineland separated from Germany (French brief) | Allied occupation of the left bank, a demilitarised zone and an Anglo-American guarantee (chosen)
Outcome: The treaty, signed on 28 June 1919, provided Allied occupation of the left bank with bridgeheads, a 50-km demilitarised zone and the Anglo-American guarantee. Germany lost about 10 percent of its prewar European territory and all overseas possessions, and under Article 231 accepted responsibility for the war and liability for reparations, set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks. The U.S. Senate voted the treaty down on 19 November 1919 and again fell seven votes short on 19 March 1920, rejecting the guarantee for which Clemenceau had given up the Rhineland; the United States signed a separate Treaty of Berlin on 25 August 1921.
Disputed points: Keynes argued the economic clauses stymied European recovery, while Foch called the treaty "a truce for 20 years". Britannica notes it was mild compared with Germany’s terms to Russia at Brest-Litovsk. Tara Finn (GOV.UK) writes that the conference was not about reconciliation and that Hitler exploited German resentment. How far the treaty caused later conflict is not settled by these sources.
Analogy limits: Coalition peace among several victors, not a single victor | The guarantee depended on another country’s legislature | Defeated state’s compliance was uncertain | Domestic leaders attacked the negotiator from the hard-line side | victor coalition in 1919 | secret-agreement diplomacy | League-era assumptions about enforcement
Horizon: Months (January–June 1919) | the conference convened in January 1919; terms settled over subsequent months
Research notes: MERGED. My pass supplies the specific Rhineland decision and the guarantee (the other pass flagged these as not covered); the other pass supplies the Big Four context, territorial and reparations terms and the March 1920 Senate vote. The two Senate votes (19 Nov 1919, 49–35; 19 Mar 1920, seven short) are both real and complementary. No scholarly monograph opened.

Decision moment: Selecting a cabinet containing political rivals
Problem: A fractured governing coalition contained powerful former competitors.
Response: Placed several rivals and strong personalities in senior posts.
When J should retrieve: A leader must choose between capable critics and personal loyalists.
Outcome / caveat: The 'team of rivals' framing can over-personalize cabinet formation and should be tested against scholarship.
Decision: Whether to fill the most important cabinet posts with his chief rivals for the 1860 nomination and with former Democrats, rather than with loyalists.
Context before: Lincoln won the 1860 Republican nomination over a field headed by William H. Seward, and Seward, Chase, Bates and Cameron had all run against him. His election was quickly followed by the secession of seven Southern states. The men available to him were more educated, better known and more experienced in government than he was. Cameron’s possible appointment was problematic because of his stained reputation.
Goals: lead the nation through the crisis | build coalitions across factions | bring diverse skills and perspectives into the cabinet
Available information: the rivals' experience and national standing | the factional geography of the remaining Union | the precedent value of cabinet appointments
Unknowns at the time: whether the rivals would cooperate with a president they resented | how the cabinet would function under war conditions
Constraints: secession crisis | factional and regional balance | need for bipartisan (former Democratic) support
Options: Appoint former Republican rivals to the three most important posts (chosen: Seward, Chase, Bates) | Appoint former Democrats to build bipartisan support (chosen: Welles, Blair, later Stanton) | Consult Republican senators before deciding on Chase (chosen as part of the process)
Outcome: Seward became secretary of state, Chase treasury secretary and Bates attorney general, and Cameron grudgingly accepted the War Department. Lincoln took the oath of office on 4 March 1861. The secretaries at first resented his success but came to respect his political skill, and the cabinet played a crucial role in his main decisions, from Fort Sumter in 1861 to the Emancipation Proclamation and the final campaign to Appomattox.
Disputed points: The "team of rivals" framing comes from Doris Kearns Goodwin’s book and the film Lincoln. The White House Historical Association presents the appointments as deliberate coalition-building across factions and regions; the Library of Congress judges that Lincoln skilfully used his cabinet’s strengths. No scholar critical of the framing was opened.
Analogy limits: 1861 American party politics | a civil-war-scale crisis | electoral legitimacy absent in non-democracies
Horizon: several months, late 1860 to March 1861
Research notes: MERGED: White House Historical Association (other pass) and Library of Congress (mine). WHHA lists Stanton among the initial "former Democrat" appointments, but Stanton replaced Cameron at War only in 1862 (roster information in my pass, not quoted) — reviewer should correct. No document shows Lincoln considering a loyalist-only cabinet, so that alternative is named in the Decision but not listed as an option.

Problem: Extreme power imbalance made candid criticism dangerous.
Response: Retained an adviser associated with a former rival and accepted repeated remonstrance.
When J should retrieve: A team needs a credible channel for dissent rather than a ceremonial request for feedback.
Outcome / caveat: Later idealization may exaggerate consistency; verify individual remonstrance episodes.
Decision: Whether to punish or to retain and promote Wei Zheng, the adviser to the brother he had just killed, as a standing critic of the throne.
Context before: In 626 Li Shimin seized the Xuanwu gate of the palace, ambushed and killed his brothers, and then informed the emperor. Wei Zheng had served a rival rebel regime and then Crown Prince Jiancheng, whom he had repeatedly urged to act early against Li Shimin. After the coup Li Shimin summoned Wei Zheng and rebuked him for dividing the brothers, and those present feared for Wei’s life. Wei answered calmly that had the crown prince followed his advice, he would not have met that day’s fate.
Goals: consolidate legitimacy after a violent succession | obtain candid advice on governance | demonstrate magnanimity
Available information: Wei Zheng's record of advice to Jiancheng | his composure and reputation | the political need to absorb the defeated faction
Unknowns at the time: whether a former rival's adviser would be loyal | how the court and the defeated faction would react | how far criticism could safely go
Constraints: post-coup factional reconciliation | the emperor's personal authority and temper | the institution of remonstrance offices
Options: Punish the defeated rival’s adviser (the danger those present feared) | Promote him to Remonstrance Official and consult him repeatedly (chosen)
Outcome: Li Shimin, moved by Wei’s composure, treated him with special courtesy and appointed him Remonstrance Official, and Gaozu abdicated in his favour two months after the coup. Taizong repeatedly consulted Wei Zheng in his private quarters; Wei submitted more than two hundred remonstrances, which Taizong said all accorded with his wishes, and Taizong credited him by name for the order of the early Zhenguan years. On Wei’s death Taizong lamented that he had lost one of his three "mirrors".
Disputed points: Britannica says it is not easy to separate the real Taizong from myths he himself encouraged. Ulrich Theobald notes that the Zhenguan zhengyao, compiled by Wu Jing, depicts an idealised virtuous ruler and served as a textbook for crown princes, so the dialogues are stylised rather than verbatim.
Analogy limits: imperial court with life-and-death power over advisers | transmitted textual tradition | Confucian remonstrance ideals
Horizon: years, from the 626 coup to Wei Zheng's death in 643
Research notes: MERGED. The other pass quotes the Zhenguan zhengyao itself (Project Gutenberg Chinese text), which supplies the rebuke, the danger of punishment, and the promotion — the rejected option that my pass could find only on Wikipedia. My pass adds Britannica’s and Theobald’s cautions. Wei Zheng’s birth year (580) is not in any opened source, so "Wei about 46" remains unsourced. Actor role: King as decision-maker; former chancellor as dissenter
Problem: Henry demanded formal acceptance of the succession settlement and repudiation of papal authority.
Response: The government imprisoned, tried, and executed More after he refused the oath as administered and denied royal supremacy.
When J should retrieve: A powerful leader is deciding whether conscientious dissent can remain inside the institution.
Outcome / caveat: Terminology needs care: More refused the 1534 succession oath because its preamble rejected papal authority; he was later convicted under the Treason Act for denying royal supremacy.
Theme tags: Dissent | Conscience | Coercion | Conscience vs. institutional loyalty | Statutory coercion
Decision: Whether to prosecute Thomas More to death for refusing the oath and denying the royal supremacy, rather than accept his partial compliance or leave him imprisoned.
Context before: More had resigned as Lord Chancellor on 16 May 1532 and retired to Chelsea. In April 1534 he was summoned to Lambeth Palace to swear the Oath of Succession, whose preamble renounced papal power and affirmed the royal supremacy. Before the king’s commissioners he declared himself willing to accept Henry’s new wife and the succession but refused to swear the oath, and he was imprisoned in the Tower on 17 April 1534.
Goals: Secure the succession and the royal supremacy | Obtain public submission from prominent figures | Henry: secure complete submission to the succession and the supremacy | More: preserve his conscience and his legal position of silence
Available information: More’s acceptance of the succession but refusal of the oath | More's stated willingness to accept the succession itself | the oath's preamble renouncing papal authority | the progress of the king's legislation
Unknowns at the time: How More’s refusal would influence others | whether More's silence would legally protect him | whether punishing him would create martyrs | what evidence could lawfully convict him
Constraints: Need for a legal basis for prosecution (Act of Treasons, November 1534) | the Act of Succession's oath requirement | the November 1534 Act of Treasons | More's standing as a former chancellor and European humanist
Options: Accept More’s acceptance of the succession and leave him imprisoned in silence | Compel his full submission | Prosecute him for treason (chosen) | Carry out the full traitor’s sentence or commute it to beheading (commuted)
Outcome: In November 1534 the Act of Treasons made malicious denial of the royal supremacy a capital offence. More was interrogated four times in the Tower, tried on 1 July 1535 on Richard Rich’s testimony that he had denied the king’s title, and sentenced to a traitor’s death that the king changed to beheading. He was executed on Tower Hill five days later, proclaiming himself "the King’s good servant but God’s first".
Disputed points: Andrea Clarke (British Library) writes that Henry demanded More’s full submission. Sources differ on the summons date: 12 April 1534 (British Library) and 13 April (Britannica). Rich’s testimony is reported by Britannica, but whether it was truthful and whether the trial was fair is not assessed in the opened sources.
Analogy limits: Religious-constitutional conflict, not ordinary disagreement | Monarch with near-absolute power | Dissenter was a former chancellor with public standing | Tudor treason law in 1534–35 | a figure of European stature | the oath's dual political-religious character
Horizon: About 15 months (April 1534–July 1535) | about fifteen months, April 1534 to July 1535
Geography: London (Lambeth Palace, Tower of London, Westminster Hall)

Problem: Unpaid officers were angry with civilian authorities and susceptible to extra-constitutional pressure.
Response: Opposed military coercion and appealed for restraint while supporting legitimate redress.
When J should retrieve: Supporters want to use coercive leverage against an institution the leader must preserve.
Outcome / caveat: Separate Washington's intervention from Congress's later financial settlement.
Decision: Whether to confront the officers’ unauthorised meeting in person and oppose coercing Congress, or let the officers’ movement proceed.
Context before: The army was in winter quarters at Newburgh, and the officers, long unpaid and anxious about arrears and retirement pay, were close to open revolt. Congress had promised half-pay in 1780, but by 1783 the states had not supplied the funds, and Congress had long been indifferent to Washington’s pleas for his men. On 10 March 1783 a meeting of officers was anonymously called, and an anonymous paper, later attributed to Major John Armstrong, urged the officers to demand rather than ask, with the implied threat of compelling Congress. Mount Vernon’s encyclopedia reports that nationalists in Philadelphia were trying to stoke the unrest to pressure Congress.
Goals: prevent an open revolt against civil authority | uphold civilian control of the military | support the officers' legitimate claims
Available information: the anonymous paper's content and its implied threat | the officers' genuine grievances | Congress's record of inaction
Unknowns at the time: whether the officers would follow the conspirators | whether Congress would act on legitimate demands | how the meeting would respond to him
Constraints: civilian supremacy as a founding principle | army unity nearing demobilization | the officers' real material distress
Options: Allow the anonymously called meeting to go ahead | Support an ultimatum to Congress as the anonymous address urged | Cancel the unofficial meeting and address the officers at an official one (chosen)
Outcome: Washington cancelled the unofficial meeting and called an official one for 15 March, where he denounced the plan as something at which "humanity revolts". He paused, put on his spectacles and some officers wept. The officers then unanimously adopted resolutions affirming confidence in Congress, asking Washington to press Congress for a speedy decision, and rejecting the anonymous address with abhorrence.

Figure(s): Florence Nightingale, the Sanitary Commission, and military authorities
Actor role: Nursing superintendent within a larger system
Problem: Overcrowded hospitals, defective drainage, disease, and supply failures drove mortality.
Response: Organized care and supplies; the Sanitary Commission later cleaned drains, improved ventilation, and addressed water and sewage conditions.
When J should retrieve: Bad outcomes may be systemic; leaders must distinguish visible frontline work from infrastructure causes.
Outcome / caveat: Disputed attribution: mortality rose during Nightingale's first winter and fell after the Commission's 1855 work; later reform credit should not be simplified to Nightingale alone.
Decision: Whether to publish her conclusion that overcrowding and defective drainage in the Scutari hospitals caused the excess deaths, or circulate it only in confidence.
Context before: In October 1854 Nightingale led an officially sanctioned party of 38 women to the Barrack Hospital at Scutari, where soldiers lay malnourished on the floor, the wounded were mixed with the infected and open latrines spread infection. She believed the sickness came mainly from exhaustion and poor nutrition, while the surgeon James Barry argued that poor sanitation and ventilation were to blame. During her first winter 4,077 soldiers died, and the death rate peaked in February 1855. A government sanitary commission arrived in March 1855, cleaned latrines and sewers and improved ventilation, after which deaths fell.
Goals: Improve army and civilian health | Reform hospital administration
Available information: Scutari mortality data for October 1854–April 1855 | The sanitary commission’s work
Unknowns at the time: How officials would react to a report blaming the hospitals
Constraints: Her position depended on government support
Options: Publish the report | Circulate it privately under confidentiality (chosen)
Outcome: In 1858 she sent a confidential report to the Minister of War blaming the excess deaths on overcrowding and defective drainage; she had copies printed and circulated under seal but never published it. She used the data to support her campaign for better civilian housing and public-health legislation in Britain and India.
Disputed points: Hugh Small (Significance) says the report would today be seen as whistleblowing and that the data could not identify which improvement caused the fall. The Science Museum gives mortality falling from 41% to 2%, Smithsonian from 42.7% to 2.2%, and Britannica says mortality under her care was much higher than had been reported. Smithsonian reports the view that she did not grasp sanitation until many thousands had died.
Analogy limits: A celebrated individual within a large bureaucracy | Disclosure could damage the army and her own hospital’s record | Nineteenth-century statistics and public health
Horizon: Months to years (1858 onward)
Research notes: KEPT MY FRAMING. The other pass kept the original decision (overhauling sanitation through the Sanitary Commission), but the commission was the government’s decision, which the original fact-check flagged; my reframe makes the decision hers. The other pass’s Science Museum evidence (Barry’s critique, 41%→2%) is merged into Context and Disputed points. Date and Age are 1858 and 37–38.

Problem: US industrial illness was poorly documented and weakly regulated.
Response: Conducted field investigations linking workplace processes to poisoning and disease.
When J should retrieve: The user suspects a systemic harm that is invisible in aggregate reporting and needs direct investigation.
Outcome / caveat: Her formal Illinois investigations began in 1910, although her interest and publication preceded them.
Decision: Whether to accept appointment to the new Illinois Occupational Diseases Commission and investigate industrial poisoning through direct field inquiry.
Context before: Hamilton had taught at Northwestern University’s Women’s Medical School since 1897 and lived at Hull House in Chicago, side by side with poor workers, where she became interested in occupational injury and illness. In 1907, exploring the foreign literature, she found that industrial medicine was barely studied in America, and in 1908 she published her first article on the subject. In 1910 she was appointed to the newly formed Occupational Diseases Commission of Illinois, the first such investigative body in the United States.
Goals: document the extent of occupational illness | raise awareness of workplace dangers | establish industrial medicine in America
Available information: European literature on industrial medicine | her community observations at Hull House | her medical and scientific training
Unknowns at the time: the extent and distribution of industrial poisoning in Illinois | which trades and processes were responsible | what regulation would follow
Constraints: absence of any prior US investigative body | weak existing regulation | limited public attention
Options: Join the commission and investigate through field inquiry and toxicology (chosen)
Outcome: Relying on "shoe leather epidemiology" and toxicology, she carried out investigations, the best known on carbon monoxide poisoning in steelworkers and mercury poisoning in hatters. In 1919 she became the first woman appointed to the Harvard Medical School faculty, and from 1924 to 1930 she was the only woman on the League of Nations Health Committee.
Disputed points: The CDC says her findings were so persuasive that they caused sweeping reforms. No dissenting assessment was opened in either pass.
Analogy limits: 1910 Progressive-era reform | a field with no prior US institutions | settlement-house social networks
Horizon: about a decade, 1907 to 1919
Research notes: MERGED: NLM (both passes) and CDC MMWR (mine). No rejected alternative is documented in either pass. Age approximate (40–41; NLM gives birth year only; the other pass used 27 Feb 1869, unsourced). ACS landmark page returned no content.

Problem: The spacecraft was crippled and power, water, oxygen, and time were constrained.
Response: Abandoned the lunar objective, conserved resources, and improvised a safe-return plan.
When J should retrieve: The original objective is no longer viable; preserve essential capabilities and redefine success.
Outcome / caveat: Collective NASA case; Gene Kranz is a useful label but not a sole decision-maker.
Decision: Whether to bring the crippled spacecraft home by a direct abort using the service-module engine, or by restoring a free-return trajectory around the Moon with the lunar module as a lifeboat.
Context before: On 13 April 1970, about 200,000 miles from Earth and en route to the Moon, oxygen tank No. 2 blew up and caused tank No. 1 to fail, and the command module lost its normal supply of electricity, light and water. A direct abort could be done only by jettisoning the lunar module and making a 6,079 ft/s burn with the service-module engine, which might have been damaged. The lunar module was built for a 45-hour lifetime and would need to last about 90, and landing had to occur while it still had enough oxygen, water and power.
Goals: return the crew safely to Earth | conserve power, water and oxygen | keep the command module viable for re-entry
Available information: the fuel-cell and oxygen status | the LM's consumables (ample oxygen; 2,181 ampere-hours of batteries; water the main concern) | Apollo 11 data on LM thermal endurance without water cooling
Unknowns at the time: whether the cold, powered-down command module could be restarted for re-entry | how long consumables would last | the effects of debris on navigation
Constraints: the LM was designed for two men for 45 hours and now had to support three for about 90 | incompatible carbon-dioxide canisters between the two modules | navigation without star sightings
Options: Direct abort with the service-module engine, jettisoning the lunar module | Restore a free-return trajectory using the lunar module (chosen; 35-second burn about five hours after the explosion) | Later PC+2 burn to shorten the return (chosen)
Outcome: The lunar landing was abandoned and the crew sheltered in the lunar module. The spacecraft looped around the Moon and splashed down in the Pacific at 1:07 p.m. on 17 April 1970, after 5 days, 22 hours and 54 minutes. NASA calls the mission a "successful failure"; the review traced the explosion to thermostatic switches not rated for 65-volt heater power, which probably welded shut.
Disputed points: No historians’ disagreement was opened. Goodman describes the trajectory choice in the passive voice, and the NASA mission page names Lunney and Lousma only for the lifeboat instruction, so the sources do not name a single decision-maker.
Analogy limits: life-critical engineering under extreme constraint | a designed-for-two vehicle housing three | 1970 NASA institutional capacity
Horizon: about four days, 13 to 17 April 1970
Geography: cislunar space and Mission Control, Houston
Research notes: MERGED. My pass found Goodman (2009, NASA NTRS), which documents the rejected direct-abort option; the other pass’s NASA page "does not mention a direct abort" (checked). The other pass supplies the 35-second burn, LM lifetime and cause. No individual main figure.

Figure(s): Steve Bales, Jack Garman, Mission Control, and the Apollo 11 crew
Actor role: Guidance officer supported by back-room specialists
Problem: Computer alarms appeared during a time-critical landing.
Response: Bales relayed a 'go' assessment after Garman and the guidance team recognized that the computer was recovering and retaining critical tasks.
When J should retrieve: A warning may be tolerable if relevant specialists can diagnose it and monitor recurrence.
Outcome / caveat: Use Bales rather than Armstrong as the focal decision figure, while preserving team credit.
Decision: Whether to call an abort of the lunar landing when unfamiliar 1202 and 1201 computer alarms sounded during descent.
Context before: Before the mission Bales had asked his deputy Jack Garman to draw up a list of computer alarm codes and what they meant. During the final descent, repeated jobs to process radar data that was not really there filled the guidance computer’s limited memory, which had only 36,864 words of fixed and 2,048 of erasable memory, and triggered a 1202 alarm, later a 1201. Each time, the computer rebooted and restarted critical tasks such as steering the descent engine. The crew had never seen the alarm in training, and the question of whether to abort reached Bales, who immediately called Garman.
Goals: land the lunar module safely | avoid an unnecessary abort
Available information: the alarm's cause (spurious radar jobs exhausting core sets) | the computer's restart behavior preserving critical functions | MIT's extensive prior testing of the restart capability
Unknowns at the time: whether the alarms would become continuous | the remaining workload and fuel margin | what the alarms meant for guidance accuracy
Constraints: time-critical descent | the computer's fixed memory capacity | crew workload during landing
Options: Abort the landing | Continue the descent (chosen)
Outcome: Garman identified the 1202 as a warning of temporary computer overload and told Bales, who told the flight director, and the landing continued. Eagle landed at 4:17 p.m. EDT on 20 July 1969 with about 30 seconds of fuel left.
Disputed points: Emphasis differs: the MIT engineer Peter Adler credits Mission Control’s confidence to MIT’s extensive testing of the restart capability and does not name Bales or Garman, while NASA’s obituary says the 25-year-old Garman "found himself making a key decision". Credit is shared across the MIT software team, Garman and Bales.
Analogy limits: 1969 real-time computing constraints | a uniquely rehearsed mission architecture | expert back-room support
Horizon: minutes, during the lunar descent of 20 July 1969
Geography: lunar descent and Mission Control, Houston
Research notes: MERGED: Adler’s ALSJ commentary (other pass; checked) explains the technical cause; NASA and Space.com (mine) document the Bales–Garman go-call chain that the other pass could not confirm. The air-to-ground transcript was not opened.

Problem: A covert invasion plan depended on weakly tested assumptions about support, secrecy, and escalation.
Response: Authorized an operation that failed to achieve its objective.
When J should retrieve: A compelling plan rests on assumptions that insiders are reluctant to challenge.
Outcome / caveat: Causal accounts and responsibility should preserve institutional and predecessor-administration context.
Decision: Whether to authorise the CIA-planned invasion of Cuba by exiles that he had inherited from the Eisenhower administration.
Context before: Eisenhower had approved the programme in March 1960, and the CIA had trained a small army of exiles in Guatemala. The plan assumed that the Cuban people and parts of the Cuban military would support the invasion. Its preparations were common knowledge among exiles in Miami, and Castro had learned of the camps by October 1960. Kennedy was determined to disguise U.S. support, and the remote Bay of Pigs landing site, more than 80 miles from refuge in the Escambray Mountains, was chosen as part of the deception. His adviser Arthur Schlesinger warned that however well disguised, any action would be ascribed to the United States and that overt intervention would have almost irreparable political consequences.
Goals: overthrow Castro and install a non-communist government | disguise U.S. support for the operation | demonstrate resolve early in the administration
Available information: the CIA plan and its stated assumptions of popular support | the semi-public status of the preparations | Castro's knowledge of the camps
Unknowns at the time: whether the Cuban population would rise up | whether U.S. involvement could stay hidden | the strength and location of Castro's forces
Constraints: the requirement for plausible deniability | the landing site's geography, over 80 miles from the Escambray refuge | the 1,400-man force size
Options: Authorise the invasion (chosen, February 1961) | Hold back until every alternative was exhausted (urged by Schlesinger)
Outcome: After the 15 April air strike exposed U.S. support, Kennedy cancelled a second strike. Brigade 2506 landed on 17 April; Cuban planes sank two escort ships and destroyed half the exile air support, and Castro sent about 20,000 troops toward the beach. Kennedy authorised an "air-umbrella" at dawn on 19 April, but the brigade was defeated within two days, with almost 1,200 surrendering and more than 100 killed. The prisoners were released in December 1962 for $53 million in food and medicine, the failure strengthened Castro, and the administration launched Operation Mongoose.
Disputed points: No historians’ disagreement was opened. The interpretive content is Schlesinger’s contemporary warnings (FRUS docs 43 and 86); the "groupthink" debate the other pass mentions has no opened source.
Analogy limits: 1961 superpower rivalry | covert-action constraints | an inherited plan meeting a new decision-maker
Horizon: about three months from authorization to the failed landing, February to April 1961
Geography: Washington, DC and the Bay of Pigs, Cuba
Research notes: MERGED: JFK Library (both passes; the other pass’s air-umbrella and escort-ship details were checked and are on the page), State Department milestone and FRUS Schlesinger memos (mine). Schlesinger’s 10 April memo post-dates the February authorisation; treat the decision as authorisation renewed up to the landing.

Problem: Cholera transmission was contested during a lethal outbreak.
Response: Mapped cases, investigated water exposure, and supported disabling a suspected pump while evidence remained incomplete.
When J should retrieve: The cost of delay is high and a targeted, reversible intervention can accompany further investigation.
Outcome / caveat: The pump-handle story is often simplified; transmission patterns and the decision process require careful sourcing.
Theme tags: Evidence | Reversible intervention | Advocacy | Outbreak investigation | Precautionary intervention
Decision: Whether to urge the parish Board of Guardians to disable the Broad Street pump before his evidence on cholera transmission was conclusive.
Context before: A recurrent cholera epidemic began in Soho on 31 August 1854, when the prevailing theory held that cholera spread through bad air, or miasma. Snow suspected the Broad Street pump, reviewed death records and interviewed households, and found that most of those who died had lived near the pump and drunk its water. When he examined the water, however, he found so little organic impurity that he hesitated to come to a conclusion.
Goals: Stop the outbreak | Test his waterborne theory | test the waterborne theory of cholera transmission
Available information: Spatial clustering of deaths around the pump | Inconclusive water examination | mapped deaths clustered around the pump | interviews documenting that most of the deceased had drunk its water | death records
Unknowns at the time: Whether the pump was the source | Whether the outbreak was already ending | whether the pump water still contained the active agent | the true cause of cholera | whether removal would end the outbreak
Constraints: He had no authority himself; the parish Board decided | Prevailing miasma theory | the prevailing miasma theory | incomplete evidence at the time of the decision | the officials' decision authority
Options: Urge removal of the pump handle (chosen) | Leave the pump in service while investigation continued (his initial hesitation)
Outcome: Snow met the Board of Guardians of St James’s parish on the evening of 7 September 1854, and the handle was removed the next day. Within two or three days fresh attacks became very few. The Rev. Henry Whitehead later found the probable cause of the contamination, and the cause of cholera remained debated until Vibrio cholerae was isolated in 1883.
Disputed points: Effect of the removal: the CDC (2004) states it "prevented additional cholera deaths", but Snow himself wrote that attacks "had been diminished before this measure was adopted", so the CDC claim is contradicted by the primary source. Brody, Rip, Vinten-Johansen, Paneth and Rachman (The Lancet, 2000) argue that modern writers repeat an apocryphal version of the story.
Analogy limits: Advocate, not decision-maker | Cheap, reversible intervention | Outbreak may already have been declining | 1854 pre-germ-theory epidemiology | a dense urban neighborhood | a reversible, low-cost intervention
Horizon: Days (early September 1854) | about a week, 31 August to 8 September 1854
Research notes: MERGED. The other pass relied on the CDC’s traditional causal claim and flagged Snow’s 1855 report as unopened; my pass quotes Snow’s 1855 text (via UCLA), which contradicts the CDC on the epidemic’s decline — recorded as a "contradicts" evidence row. The decision-maker is the Board, on Snow’s advice.

Problem: A drug application faced unresolved evidence and pressure for approval.
Response: Withheld approval and required adequate safety evidence.
When J should retrieve: Potential harm is large or irreversible and commercial urgency is being mistaken for proof.
Outcome / caveat: Federal regulatory case, not a personal-scale decision.
Theme tags: Regulation | Evidence threshold | Pressure | Regulatory gatekeeping | Evidence standards
Decision: Whether to let the thalidomide application be approved, or keep demanding more evidence of safety despite company pressure.
Context before: Kelsey joined the FDA on 1 August 1960 as one of a handful of medical officers reviewing new drug applications, and received the thalidomide application in early September 1960. The drug was already available in dozens of countries. Under the rules then, the FDA had sixty days after receipt to reject an application, and she judged its claims too glowing for the clinical support offered. After a report of peripheral neuritis, the FDA asked the company for more information and proof of safety, which led to questions about use in pregnancy.
Goals: Ensure drug safety | Meet the review deadline lawfully | ensure adequate safety evidence before marketing approval | protect the public from unproven drugs
Available information: The application’s clinical data | Reports of peripheral neuritis | the application's contents and their inadequacy | her pharmacological training and prior review experience | the requirement for safety evidence under then-current law
Unknowns at the time: Effects of the drug in pregnancy | Long-term toxicity | the drug's effects on pregnant women and fetuses | its long-term safety | how long the company would press
Constraints: Sixty-day review rule | Company pressure | constant company pressure | the drug's established presence abroad | the pre-1962 regulatory framework
Options: Approve, or let the application lapse into approval | Find it deficient and demand more evidence (chosen)
Outcome: The company resubmitted repeatedly and kept pressing, while she insisted on scientifically reliable evidence. About a year later, researchers in Germany and Australia linked thalidomide to clusters of severe birth defects, and on 30 November 1961 Merrell told the FDA that the German firm was withdrawing the drug. It was never marketed in the US, the episode helped pass the 1962 Drug Amendments, and Kennedy gave Kelsey the President’s Award in 1962.
Disputed points: No disagreement was opened. The judgement that the claims outran the data is Kelsey’s own (Autobiographical Reflections).
Analogy limits: Regulator with legal power to withhold | Harm discovered abroad during the delay | Mid-century drug law | 1960–61 U.S. drug regulation | a drug already marketed abroad | irreversible potential harm
Horizon: About 15 months (September 1960–November 1961) | about a year, September 1960 to late 1961
Research notes: MERGED: FDA exhibit (both passes), Kelsey’s Autobiographical Reflections and NLM (mine). Birth date 24 July 1914 (other pass) not verified in an opened source; age approximate. The March 1962 withdrawal of the application (in older summaries) was not found in either pass.

Figure(s): Ernest Shackleton and the Endurance expedition
Problem: Loss of the ship made the original expedition impossible.
Response: Reorganized the mission around survival, movement, and rescue.
When J should retrieve: A leader must explicitly abandon an obsolete objective and reset team expectations.
Outcome / caveat: Avoid heroic simplification; decisions and labor were distributed across the expedition.
Decision: Whether to leave most of the party on Elephant Island and sail the James Caird 800 miles to South Georgia for help, or wait together on the island.
Context before: The expedition had set out to cross Antarctica from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea. Endurance was locked in the ice on 19 January 1915 and gradually crushed over the next nine months. The men camped for five months on the ice and, when it broke up, reached Elephant Island in the three boats. The island was more than 800 miles from the nearest inhabited land with people who could help, and Shackleton knew there were Norwegian whaling stations on the north side of South Georgia.
Goals: bring every man home alive | reach inhabited land and organize rescue
Available information: the Norwegian whaling stations on the north side of South Georgia | the three boats and their condition | the men's physical state
Unknowns at the time: whether the small open boat could survive the Southern Ocean | the weather in the Drake Passage | whether those left behind could survive indefinitely
Constraints: 800 miles of the world's most dangerous ocean | the boat's size and sailing qualities | the approaching Antarctic winter
Options: Wait on Elephant Island | Sail the James Caird with five others to South Georgia (chosen)
Outcome: After 15 days at sea the James Caird sighted South Georgia. Shackleton, Crean and Worsley crossed the island’s unmapped mountains, climbing nearly 3,000 feet and marching for about 36 hours, to reach the Stromness whaling station. The men left on Elephant Island were picked up on 30 August 1916 by a Chilean navy tug, and all were rescued.
Disputed points: The sinking date conflicts between sources: Royal Museums Greenwich gives 27 October 1915, while the Scott Polar Research Institute says the ship sank in November 1915. RMG reports that all the men believed their survival was due largely to Shackleton’s leadership; the crew’s distributed labour is easily lost in heroic retellings.
Analogy limits: 1916 open-boat navigation limits | an uninhabited starting point | no radio contact with the outside world
Horizon: the boat journey decision followed months adrift; the voyage itself lasted 15 days
Geography: Elephant Island and the Southern Ocean to South Georgia
Research notes: MERGED: RMG (both passes) and SPRI (mine). Sinking date deliberately left out of Context because the two sources conflict (27 October is commonly given as the date the ship was abandoned — reviewer check). The James Caird departure (24 April 1916) and landfall dates are in neither opened source. Age 42 (1916). Original Date column updated to 1916.

Figure(s): Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace
Problem: Darwin had accumulated evidence for years when Wallace independently sent a similar theory.
Response: Accepted a joint presentation and then completed a book-length public argument.
When J should retrieve: Long preparation meets a trigger that raises the cost of further delay.
Outcome / caveat: Deduplicated: one Darwin decision moment only; priority and credit require careful treatment.
Decision: Whether Darwin's material should be presented jointly with Wallace's essay at the Linnean Society, with Darwin's consent, as arranged by Lyell and Hooker.
Context before: The year 1858 opened with Darwin hard at work on his 'big book' on species, begun in May 1856 at Lyell's urging and already more than half finished. In mid-June 1858, as he began writing up his study of pigeons, his work was interrupted by the arrival of Wallace's letter, enclosing an essay enunciating Wallace's own theory of natural selection. Darwin's shock is evident in his letter to Lyell: 'I never saw a more striking coincidence. if Wallace had my M.S. sketch written out in 1842 he could not have made a better short abstract!' Lyell and Hooker suggested that Darwin's years of labour be acknowledged by publishing jointly with Wallace's paper part of an early sketch of his theory, together with an abstract of his views sent to Asa Gray in September 1857.
Goals: acknowledge Darwin's years of work while doing justice to Wallace | settle the priority question fairly | advance science
Available information: Darwin's 1844 sketch and his 1857 letter to Asa Gray | Wallace's essay | the Linnean Society's meeting schedule
Unknowns at the time: how Wallace would react to the arrangement | how the joint presentation would be received | the implications for Darwin's larger work
Constraints: the Society's final meeting before the summer recess, set for 1 July | Darwin's family crises — diphtheria, scarlet fever and the death of his baby on 28 June | the unfinished state of the 'big book'
Options: arrange a joint presentation at the Linnean Society with Darwin's consent (chosen) | let Wallace's paper be published alone while Darwin continued the big book (the implicit alternative)
Outcome: The papers were read at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858; Darwin, overwhelmed by family illness, did not attend. The correspondence includes Wallace's letter thanking Lyell and Hooker for their 'kind offices on this occasion'. Darwin then began the 'abstract' that became On the Origin of Species, published in November 1859.
Disputed points: When Darwin actually received Wallace's letter is disputed: Brooks and McKinney have argued for earlier receipt, while Beddall concluded the question of whether Darwin held the letter up for any reason is 'essentially unresolvable'; credit-sharing between Darwin, Lyell and Hooker is also debated in the historiography (as summarized by the Darwin Correspondence Project).
Analogy limits: 1858 scientific priority norms | a small London scientific society's procedures | the private-unpublished-work system of the day
Horizon: about two weeks, mid-June to 1 July 1858
Research notes: FROM THE OTHER PASS ONLY (not researched in mine). Note: the canonical workbook lists C26 as Expansion, not Core; the other pass labelled it Core. Kept the other pass’s content unchanged; evidence rows not re-checked. Original notes: Ages computed from standard birth dates. The opened source (Darwin Correspondence Project) documents the sequence, the joint arrangement, and the dating dispute; Wallace's own reaction beyond his letter of thanks is not covered, and the Linnean Society's own account was located in search but not opened. Per the audit repair, the arrangers (Lyell and Hooker) are treated as the decision's movers with Darwin consenting and Wallace informed after the fact.

Decision moment: 'Moving the wooden pole to establish trust'
Problem: A government planning major legal reforms lacked public credibility.
Response: A traditional account says he paid a conspicuous reward for a simple public task before promulgating reforms.
When J should retrieve: A small, observable promise kept may build credibility before a costly change.
Outcome / caveat: Treat as a transmitted historical anecdote, not a verified behavioral experiment.
Decision: Whether to stage a conspicuous, immediately rewarded public act to show the state would keep its word before promulgating the new laws.
Context before: According to Sima Qian’s Shiji (ch. 68), after Duke Xiao of Qin employed Shang Yang, Shang Yang wished to change the laws but feared criticism from all under heaven. After a court debate the duke approved, appointed him Zuo Shuzhang, and the reform edict was settled. The edict was prepared but not yet promulgated, and Shang Yang feared the people would not believe it.
Goals: establish the credibility of the new orders | implement the reform program effectively
Available information: the visible distrust of government pronouncements | the outcome of the court debate | the ruler's backing
Unknowns at the time: whether the people would respond to the reward | whether the gesture would translate into compliance
Constraints: the need for the edict to take effect | popular skepticism of official promises | the scale of the coming legal changes
Options: Erect a pole with a public reward for moving it before issuing the decree (chosen) | Promulgate the decree directly (the implicit alternative)
Outcome: According to the Shiji, a pole three zhang tall was set up at the south gate of the capital market with ten gold offered for moving it to the north gate; no one dared, so the reward was raised to fifty gold, one man moved it and was paid at once, "to show there was no deception", and the decree was then issued. When the crown prince later broke the new law, his tutor and teacher were punished in his place and the next day the people complied; the Shiji says that after ten years the people were pleased and the towns and villages well ordered.
Disputed points: Historicity: the episode survives only in the Shiji, written long after the events. Yuri Pines judges Sima Qian’s biography "not entirely reliable" but "not pure fiction", and Sima Qian himself called Shang Yang harsh by nature. Britannica and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy do not mention the pole story. Dating differs: tradition places the reforms c. 356 BCE, while Pines dates their launch to 359 BCE.
Analogy limits: Warring States reform politics | a single transmitted chronicle | a public-credibility mechanism hard to stage today
Horizon: days, within the reform program traditionally dated c. 356 BCE
Geography: the Qin capital's market (south gate to north gate)

Decision moment: Battle of Julu and destruction of retreat options
Problem: An army faced a high-stakes fight under morale and coordination pressure.
Response: Traditional accounts describe breaking cooking vessels and sinking boats to remove retreat options.
When J should retrieve: Irreversible commitment may concentrate effort when the actor controls the risk and the strategy is otherwise sound.

Decision: Whether to destroy the army’s boats and cooking vessels and carry only three days’ rations to force a decisive battle to relieve the siege of Julu.
Context before: According to Sima Qian’s Shiji (ch. 7), the Chu relief army under Song Yi halted at Anyang for forty-six days without advancing. Xiang Yu beheaded Song Yi in his tent at dawn and announced that the king of Chu had secretly ordered it. The allied armies that had come to relieve Julu stayed behind their walls and did not engage.
Goals: relieve the siege of Julu and destroy the Qin army | secure supreme command | motivate a badly supplied, freezing army
Available information: Song Yi's forty-six days of inaction and the army's suffering | the siege situation at Julu | the allies' armies encamped nearby
Unknowns at the time: whether the outnumbered troops could win | whether the allied armies watching from their ramparts would join the fight | whether the men could survive on three days' rations

Problem: After defeat, the Continental Army risked encirclement and destruction at Brooklyn Heights.
Response: Ordered a secret nighttime evacuation across the East River, preserving the army.

Decision: Whether to evacuate the army from Brooklyn Heights across the East River before the British could surround it, or hold the lines on Long Island.
Context before: On 27 August 1776 British forces under Howe, who had led about 10,000 men through the unguarded Jamaica Pass, defeated the advanced elements of Washington’s army. Howe halted the fighting and had his men dig trenches around the American position the next day. About 9,500 men held the weakly fortified camp on Brooklyn Heights, and Washington feared British warships might enter the East River and cut his communications with New York. On 29 August a council of war considered whether to leave Long Island, citing the lost ground, the loss of officers, rain that had damaged arms, and ships attempting to enter the river.
Goals: save the army from defeat and capture | preserve the capacity to continue the war | avoid encirclement in a false position
Available information: Howe's decision to besiege rather than assault | the army's exposed position with the East River at its back | the availability of boats
Unknowns at the time: whether the Royal Navy would enter the East River | whether the night crossing could stay undetected | whether the weather would hold
Constraints: the Royal Navy's control of the waters | night navigation in small boats | the army's morale after defeat
Options: Hold Brooklyn Heights | Leave Long Island by night (chosen; council of war unanimous)
Outcome: From late on 29 August to dawn the next morning the troops were rowed back to Manhattan; a dense fog covered the last crossings, and the British did not realise the army had gone until it was complete. According to eyewitnesses, Washington was the last man to leave. He reported to Congress on 31 August that he had lost no men, ammunition or supplies in the operation.

Problem: Rome faced a superior battlefield commander after severe defeats.
Response: Avoided a decisive battle, shadowed Hannibal, and sought to preserve Roman capacity.
When J should retrieve: The opponent benefits from immediate confrontation and time may improve the user's position.
Outcome / caveat: Birth year is uncertain, conventionally around 280 BCE; age must remain approximate.
Decision: Whether, as dictator after the disaster at Lake Trasimene, to refuse a decisive battle with Hannibal and shadow him instead.
Context before: Livy records that in 217 BCE Hannibal destroyed the consul Flaminius’s army at Lake Trasimene, with fifteen thousand Romans killed. Livy calls it a disaster for Rome memorable as few others have been. In this emergency the citizens turned to a long-unused remedy, a dictatorship, and Quintus Fabius Maximus was given dictatorial powers with Minucius Rufus as master of horse.
Goals: preserve the Roman state's military capacity | contain Hannibal's advance | avoid a third catastrophic defeat
Available information: the lesson of Flaminius's rashness at Trasimene | Hannibal's superiority in open battle | the state of Roman manpower and morale
Unknowns at the time: how long a strategy of delay could be sustained politically | the loyalty of Rome's allies as their lands were ravaged | Hannibal's own plans
Constraints: Roman expectations of decisive battle | the devastation of allied territory under Hannibal | the master of horse's public opposition
Options: Refuse a general engagement, keep to high ground, shadow and harass (chosen) | Offer battle, as Minucius urged
Outcome: Fabius kept to high ground at a moderate distance, never losing sight of the enemy and never closing with him, while small encounters on safe ground restored his men’s confidence; Livy says Hannibal saw he faced a very different kind of commander. Minucius openly abused him, calling his deliberation indolence and his caution cowardice, and was later given equal authority, fought on unfavourable ground and put his legions in great peril. At Cannae, under later commanders, 45,000 Romans were killed.
Disputed points: The narrative comes from Livy (Book 22), writing under Augustus. Livy himself contrasts contemporary scorn with later vindication. Britannica notes "Cunctator" was a nickname, not his official cognomen.
Analogy limits: 217 BCE Roman politics and manpower | an allied system being tested | a commander's six-month dictatorship
Horizon: months, the dictatorship of 217 BCE

Problem: A larger invading fleet threatened the Greek alliance.
Response: Helped draw the Persian fleet into confined waters favorable to the Greek navy.
When J should retrieve: A narrower, well-chosen arena can convert a scale disadvantage into a tactical advantage.
Outcome / caveat: Born around 524 BCE, so age at Salamis is approximate; do not state 54.
Decision: Whether the Greek fleet should fight the Persians in the strait at Salamis, or withdraw to the Isthmus as most of the allied commanders urged.
Context before: According to Herodotus (Book 8), after Artemisium the Greek fleet came to Salamis at the Athenians’ request so they could evacuate their families. At the council of war most speakers advised sailing to the Isthmus to fight for the Peloponnese, since defeat at Salamis would leave them trapped on an island. The Athenian Mnesiphilus warned Themistocles that if the fleet left Salamis it would scatter and Hellas would be lost. Herodotus puts the fleet at 378 ships, while a Persian navy of about 800 galleys was nearby.
Goals: keep the allied fleet concentrated and fighting | defeat the Persian fleet | save Hellas
Available information: the majority's plan to withdraw to the Isthmus | Mnesiphilus's warning that leaving Salamis would scatter the fleet | the topographical argument that open water favored the heavier, more numerous Persian ships
Unknowns at the time: whether the allies would stay if the fleet stayed | Persian numbers and intentions | what terms Athens' evacuation implied
Constraints: Peloponnesian fortification of the Isthmus | Athenian dependence on the fleet | the alliance's fragile command structure under Eurybiades
Options: Withdraw and fight at the Isthmus (majority position) | Fight in the strait at Salamis (Themistocles, chosen by Eurybiades)
Outcome: Themistocles urged Eurybiades that it lay in his hand to save Hellas by fighting at Salamis, and threatened that the Athenians would otherwise sail to Siris in Italy; Eurybiades chose to stay and fight where they were (Herodotus 8.62–63). When the Peloponnesians were again outvoting him, Themistocles secretly sent Sicinnus to tell the Persians the Greeks were planning flight; the Persians believed it and encircled Salamis by night (8.75–76). Most Persian ships were shattered by the Athenians and Aeginetans (8.86), and Xerxes, fearing for his Hellespont bridges, planned flight (8.97). Britannica gives about 300 Persian vessels sunk for about 40 Greek, and says Xerxes had to postpone his land offensives for a year.
Disputed points: Rule 6: the account rests on Herodotus (Godley translation) and other ancient sources. Fleet sizes differ: Herodotus gives 378 Greek ships, Britannica about 370. Motive: Herodotus himself judges that Eurybiades gave way chiefly for fear of the Athenians leaving (8.63). Causation of victory: Thomas R. Martin stresses the narrow channel; Herodotus stresses Greek order versus Persian disorder (8.86). Herodotus shows the decision being reopened after 8.63 (8.75), so whether the Sicinnus ruse or Eurybiades’ decision fixed the battle site is a matter of reading.
Analogy limits: 480 BCE alliance politics | Persian invasion of a burning Attica | ancient naval combat in confined waters
Horizon: days, the council and battle of late September 480 BCE

Figure(s): Winston Churchill and the War Cabinet
Decision moment: Whether to explore mediation or negotiations
Problem: Military crisis and cabinet disagreement raised the possibility of Italian mediation.
Response: Argued against pursuing terms and continued the war.
