Theme tags: Principle under existential threat | Cabinet deliberation
Decision: Whether to explore mediation with Hitler through Mussolini, or refuse any approach implying terms and fight on.
Context before: In late May 1940 the fate of the British Expeditionary Force at Dunkirk was in the balance, and the King of the Belgians had asked the Germans for an armistice. On 26 May Halifax told the War Cabinet that the Italian ambassador had made soundings about a conference, and that he had replied Britain might discuss peace if its liberty and independence were assured. Churchill opposed any negotiations that might derogate Britain’s rights, but said he would be thankful to get out of the present difficulties on such terms and did not object to some approach being made to Mussolini. Halifax then asked whether the Prime Minister would discuss terms if Hitler offered ones that left Britain’s independence intact.
Goals: preserve Britain's complete liberty and independence | keep the French in the war | avoid being dragged into a settlement at German mercy
Available information: the ambassador's soundings and Halifax's position | the Chiefs of Staff paper on continuing the war alone | the evolving military news from France
Unknowns at the time: what terms Mussolini or Hitler might actually offer | whether America would assist | how much of the army could be evacuated from Dunkirk
Constraints: coalition politics — Churchill's new premiership and Labour's support | French pressure to approach Mussolini | Halifax's standing and possible resignation
Options: Approach Mussolini to mediate with Hitler (Halifax) | Permit a limited approach without commitment (Churchill’s position on 26 May) | Refuse any approach and fight on (chosen by 28 May)
Outcome: Over 26–28 May the War Cabinet met nine times. On 28 May Chamberlain said the present was not the time for advances to Mussolini, the War Cabinet concluded that the answer to any such offer could only be "No", and Churchill told the outer cabinet "we must decline anything like this and fight on"; Dalton recorded no dissent.
Disputed points: The Museum of the Prime Minister notes that Churchill’s memoir claim that fighting on alone "never found a place on the War Cabinet agenda" is contradicted by the minutes; the National Archives blog shows his openness on 26 May before his rejection on 28 May, which argues against a lone-hero narrative. The International Churchill Society describes Halifax as wanting to negotiate.

Geography: London (Admiralty House, 10 Downing Street, House of Commons)

Decision moment: South Pole expedition planning and execution
Problem: An extreme objective required reliable transport, depots, clothing, navigation, and pacing.
Response: Used methods and logistics closely fitted to polar conditions.
When J should retrieve: Execution risk is dominated by preparation, system fit, and operational margin.
Outcome / caveat: Contrast with Scott must not erase different routes, aims, luck, or disputed causal explanations.
Theme tags: Timing | Rivalry | Reversibility | Preparation margin | Logistics fit
Decision: Whether to start for the Pole in early September 1911, before the worst of the winter cold was over, or wait for warmer conditions.
Context before: After Peary and Cook both claimed the North Pole in 1909, Amundsen turned his expedition to the South Pole, keeping the decision secret even from his crew. His base at the Bay of Whales was 96 km nearer the Pole than Scott’s at Ross Island, and he arrived on 14 January 1911 with 116 dogs and laid 3,000 kg of supplies in depots at 80°, 81° and 82°S. He worried that Scott might set off first and gain distance with motor sledges. On 7 September the temperature rose into the minus twenties.
Goals: Reach the Pole first | Protect men and dogs | achieve a polar first | keep the expedition funded and intact | reach the Pole before any rival
Available information: Depot positions | Weather on 7 September | Scott’s motor sledges | the Peary and Cook claims that removed the North Pole's value | his Inuit-learned techniques of dog driving, clothing and polar survival | knowledge of Scott's rival expedition
Unknowns at the time: Whether the warm spell would last | When Scott would start | whether the Bay of Whales route was viable | the severity of the coming season | Scott's progress and motor sledges
Constraints: Antarctic winter conditions | Rivalry with Scott | the need for secrecy to preserve funding and the loan of the Fram | the Antarctic season | the rival British expedition
Options: Wait for warmer conditions | Start the next day, 8 September (chosen)
Outcome: On 11 September the party woke to −55°C and turned back from the 80°S depot; men suffered frostbite and Prestrud nearly died. After Johansen publicly accused Amundsen, he was removed from the Pole party. Five men restarted on 20 October with four sledges of 13 dogs each, reached the Pole on 14 December 1911, spent three days verifying the position, and returned to Framheim on 26 January 1912 after 99 days and about 3,000 km.
Disputed points: The Fram Museum attributes the early start to Amundsen’s worry about Scott and records Johansen’s public accusation; how far this reflects on Amundsen’s leadership is interpretation. Comparisons with Scott that credit preparation alone must account for routes, aims, luck and weather.

Decision: Whether to press on to the Pole by man-hauling after sending the dog teams back, and then attempt the return.
Context before: Scientific investigation lay at the heart of the British Antarctic Expedition. In Melbourne in October 1910 Scott received Amundsen’s telegram: "Beg inform you Fram proceeding antarctic." Scott and 11 others started overland for the Pole from Cape Evans on 24 October 1911 with motor sledges, ponies and dogs, and the dog teams were later sent back.
Goals: Reach the Pole | Return safely | reach the South Pole | carry out the scientific and meteorological program | bring the polar party home
Available information: Transport performance so far | the meteorological and scientific program design | Amundsen's telegram announcing the rival bid | the expedition's transport preparations
Unknowns at the time: Weather on the return | Whether Amundsen had already reached the Pole | the weather that would be met on the return journey | the reliability of transport and depot margins | the rival's progress
Constraints: Food and fuel limits | Man-hauling effort | logistics over hundreds of miles of ice barrier and glacier | the Antarctic season's closing window | the competing scientific obligations
Options: Press on toward the Pole by man-hauling and attempt the return (chosen)
Outcome: A five-man party reached the Pole on 17 January 1912 and found that Amundsen had preceded them by about a month. Evans died on 17 February and Oates on 17 March. In his last entry on 29 March Scott wrote of a continuous gale since the 21st, fuel and food for two days, and a depot 11 miles away they could not reach for drift; the last three died there. Their meteorological log was found with their bodies.
Disputed points: Science News reports that scholars have often blamed Scott’s poor planning; against this, the expedition meteorologist George Simpson concluded (Met Office) that the party met exceptionally low temperatures on the return, and Susan Solomon and Charles Stearns found temperatures below −30°F for nearly a month in February–March 1912, about 10° below recent averages.
